newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Long winter delays Russian grain belt crop sowing.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Long winter delays Russian grain belt crop sowing.

text.p: A longer than usual winter in Russia's fertile Kuban region has delayed spring planting and could hurt this year's output in the country's grain belt, regional officials say.
"Last year was bad and we have already begun extremely poorly; spring is a month behind schedule," Nikolai Kondratenko, Krasnodar's pro-Communist Governor, told Reuters.
"April is already tomorrow and we cannot plant. We have begun to work with losses," he said.
The Kuban, at the foothills of the northern Caucasus mountains by the Black Sea, produces Russia's best wheat, but has suffered two years of particularly poor crops.
The region produced a net four million tons of grain and pulses in 1996, down from 10 million in 1990.
"The weather has been unfavourable and we are now three weeks late in working the fields because of cold weather," said Ivan Petrenko, deputy regional governer overseeing agriculture.
"How will this affect the wheat and other crops? I think negatively, because it limits the planting season," he said.

Parts of this region -- one of only three nationwide which made a profit from farming in 1996, according to Moscow farm officials -- are still covered with snow at a time when farms are usually already sowing crops for harvesting in autumn.

A recent tour of the countryside outside Krasnodar revealed little activity in the fields, with many farmers bundled in winter jackets working in unheated warehouses, trying to put dilapidated machinery into working order.

In one of the few signs of outdoor work a group of peasants had gathered to plant along the roadside on a small plot of dark brown earth, which, like most of the surrounding countryside, was a sea of mud.
LONG WINTER OCCURS ABOUT ONCE A DECADE
Pyotr Rybalkin, director of the Krasnodar Agriculture Institute, said such a long winter usually occurs about once a decade.
"It's hard to remember the last time things began so late," he said.
Petrenko said spring planting typically begins by March 5 or 10. "Now it's already been the end of March and we are standing still."

Kondratenko, a communist official during Soviet times and former head of the Agriculture Institute, said he was worried that wheat output could fall this year but said it was too soon to make predictions.
Russia's total grain harvest last year was 69.3 million tonnes, the second poor result in a row and one of the worst on record in three decades.
With nationwide farm grain stocks expected to be very tight in coming months, Kuban's late sowing campaign could make the time until the next harvest a lean one.
But despite the slow start, the region could still recover with a good crop if favourable weather conditions prevail in the months to come, agricultural experts say.
Kondratenko said the local government was doing all it could to help boost crops, moves he said were important because of what he called potential threats from abroad.

"We are taking measures to plant because we understand that tomorrow America or the (world's largest industrialised economies in the) G-7 will blockade the shipment of foodstuffs to Russia because they don't like our politics or internal situation in the country," he said.
"Hunger is returning to Russia. It does not have any food production any more," he said, painting a dire picture others dismiss as political hyperbole from an opponent of the Moscow government.
COLLECTIVE FARMS STRUGGLE TO COPE WITH MARKET ECONOMY
Collective farms set up under communism and now muddling through as largely unreformed joint stock corporations are struggling with ageing machinery and lacklustre management.
Poor results over the past two years have made it hard for them to buy new tractors, fertiliser and seed.
Farms have been unable to cope with the transition to a market economy and have seen output plunge, leaving imported foods to fill up to 50 percent of the domestic food market.
The era of big, Russian government-financed grain imports is over.
The number of private farms, which some believe is the long-term solution to Russia's agricultural problems, is increasingly only slowly.
Many would-be private farmers find it impossible to get loans to buy the equipment needed to set up their own farms.
As a result only about five or six percent of all farming in the Kuban is done on family farms, according to officials from AKKOR, a private farmers' group.
